slides.title: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
slides.subtitle: Long ago, a curved piece of glass shaped like a lentil seed opened a hidden world too tiny for our eyes to see.
points: Have you ever wondered what you might see if the invisible world around you became visible?
How might it change the way you think about size, complexity, or even what counts as 'living'?
Have you thought how these tiny living beings interact with each other?

slides.title: From a lentil-shaped lens to the microscope
slides.body: The human eye can only see things above a certain size, so for a long time many tiny things stayed unknown. People found that a curved piece of glass — thick in the middle, thin at the edge, shaped like a **lentil seed** — could make small things look bigger, so they called it a **lens**. Better and better lenses became the **microscope**, which finally opened a hidden world of tiny living creatures.

slides.title: Everything living is an organism
slides.body: Plants and animals come in every shape, size, and colour — some tiny, some really big. All living beings, whether plant or animal, are called **organisms**. But how small a thing can your eyes actually see? Some organisms are simply too small for the naked eye — and that is the world this chapter explores.

slides.title: A water-filled flask as a magnifier
slides.purpose: Before the microscope, how could anyone enlarge a tiny thing? We turn an everyday glass flask of **water** into a lens and test whether it really makes small things bigger.
steps: Fill — a round-bottom glass flask completely with water
Seal — close the mouth of the flask with a cork
Look — place the flask on an open book and read the letters through it; then view an ant
slides.observe: The letters look **larger** through the flask! The water-filled flask acts like a real **magnifying glass** — and through it you can see the details of a small creature, like an ant's body, far more clearly. This curiosity about tiny life eventually led to the microscope.

slides.title: Two pioneers of the microscope
slides.leftBody: In his book **Micrographia**, a careful observer and skilled artist drew tiny things never seen before. His microscope made things look **200 to 300 times** bigger. Looking at a thin slice of cork full of small empty spaces like a **honeycomb**, he named each space a **cell** — the first time the word was used in science for the basic unit of life.
slides.rightBody: A Dutch scientist who made **better lenses** for more useful microscopes. He was the first person to clearly see and describe tiny living things like **bacteria** and **blood cells** — and so is known as the **Father of Microbiology**.

slides.title: What is a cell?
slides.intro: All living beings are made up of cells. Let us take a closer look at the basic structure of a cell using a microscope.

slides.kicker: ACTIVITY 2.2 · LET US STUDY A CELL
slides.title: Mounting an onion peel (teacher demonstration)
slides.purpose: What does a plant cell actually look like? We stain and mount the thin **onion peel** so its hidden, brick-like structure shows up clearly under the microscope.
steps: Peel — pull the thin transparent layer from the inner surface of an onion piece with forceps
Stain — soak the peel in **safranin** (a red stain) for 30 seconds, then rinse in water
Mount — place it flat on a slide, add a drop of **glycerin**, and lower a coverslip at 45° so no air bubbles get trapped
Observe — view under a microscope (even a foldable paper one works) and compare with the diagram
slides.observe: You see nearly **rectangular** structures, closely arranged with no space between them — like a **wall made of bricks**. These are onion-peel cells, and they show that all plants are made up of cells.

slides.title: Looking at your own cheek cells
slides.purpose: Are animal cells like plant cells? We collect cells from the inside of your **own cheek** and compare them with the onion peel.
steps: Scrape — rinse your mouth, then gently scrape the inside of your cheek with the blunt end of a toothpick
Spread — smear the material in a drop of water on a clean slide
Stain — add a drop of **methylene blue** (a blue stain) to improve contrast, wait a minute, add glycerin and a coverslip
Observe — view under the microscope and draw what you see
slides.observe: You see **polygon-shaped** cheek cells that line the inside of your mouth. Like onion cells, each one has the same three basic parts — showing both plants and animals are built from cells.

slides.title: Membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus
slides.body: Every cell has three basic parts. The **cell membrane** is the porous outer layer that encloses the cell, separates it from others, and lets useful materials in and waste out. The **cytoplasm** fills the space inside, where most **life processes** happen and which holds carbohydrates, proteins, fats, and mineral salts. The **nucleus** is the round body in the middle that regulates all the cell's activities and its growth. Onion cells also have an extra outer **cell wall** that gives plants rigidity and strength.

slides.title: Plant cell vs animal cell
slides.leftBody: Has a **cell wall** and a large **vacuole** that stores substances and keeps the cell's shape. **Plastids** are tiny rod-shaped structures; the green ones, **chloroplasts**, hold chlorophyll for **photosynthesis**.
slides.rightBody: Has **no cell wall**; vacuoles are usually absent, or small if present. A cell is not a simple bag of liquid — it is a **complex structure** of many parts, each with its own special job, like **mitochondria**.

slides.title: Variation in shape and structure of cells
slides.intro: Do all cells look the same? A muscle cell and a nerve cell are very different — why?

slides.title: A cell's shape suits its job
slides.body: Cells look different because their shape relates to their work. A **muscle** cell is shaped like a **spindle** so it can contract; a **nerve** cell is very **long and branched** so it can carry messages quickly to different parts of the body. Inner cheek cells are thin and flat to form a protective lining, while some plant cells form long tubes that carry water through the plant.

slides.title: What are the levels of organisation in the body of a living organism?
slides.intro: The body of a living organism is organised in a complex way — from a single cell up to a whole living being.

slides.title: From a single cell to a whole organism
slides.body: Just as a **brick** is the basic unit of a wall, the **cell** is the basic unit of life — but a living body is far more than a pile of cells. A group of similar cells working together forms a **tissue**; different tissues organised for one job form an **organ**, like the **stomach**; several organs handling a major function such as **digestion** form an **organ system**; and all the organ systems together make a complete **organism**. Each level is built from the one below it, so a body is organised step by step, from a single cell up to the whole living being.

slides.title: Every complex life begins as one 'egg'
slides.body: The life of a complex organism begins with a single cell — the **'egg'**. This egg has the amazing ability to **divide again and again** to form a complete living being made of many cells. Such organisms are called **multicellular organisms** — animals, humans, and plants are all examples.

slides.title: The largest cell in the living world
slides.body: The yolk — the yellow part — of an **ostrich egg** is a single cell, the **largest known cell**, measuring about **130 mm to 170 mm** across! The egg also has non-cellular extras: a shell for protection and a white liquid that nourishes the cell as it develops.

slides.title: What are microorganisms?
slides.intro: Some living things are made of just one or very few cells — so small they cannot be seen with the naked eye. Let us meet the world of microbes.

slides.title: Living beings beyond the naked eye
slides.body: **Microorganisms** are living things made of one or very few cells, too small to see with the naked eye (**micro** means very small; **organism** means living being). Some, like bacteria and **Amoeba**, are **unicellular**; others, like some fungi and algae, are **multicellular**. They live everywhere — in water, soil, air, and even inside our own body. A low-cost **foldable paper microscope** now makes this hidden world accessible to many people.

slides.title: A drop of pond water
slides.purpose: Is ordinary pond water really 'empty'? We take a single drop and look for life that the naked eye completely misses.
steps: Collect — gather pond or stagnant water in a container with help from your teacher or elder
Drop — place one drop on a microscope slide using a dropper and cover it with a coverslip
Observe — watch for tiny moving organisms under the microscope
slides.observe: A single drop is **teeming with tiny organisms** moving about — life invisible to the unaided eye, swimming in water you would have called plain.

slides.title: Identifying four kinds of microbes
slides.purpose: After watching pond water and soil suspension, can we **name** what we saw? Students recorded their observations, then matched them with information from the library and internet to identify each microbe.
steps: Record — note the shape and movement of each organism seen in pond water (Table 2.1) and soil suspension (Table 2.2)
Compare — match your notes against reference pictures of known microbes
Group — sort them into protozoa, algae, fungi, and bacteria
slides.observe: The organisms fall into **four groups** — protozoa, algae, fungi, and bacteria. We can only see them with a microscope that magnifies **100 to 400 times**, yet small as they are, they play an important role in our lives.

slides.title: Four kinds of microbes under the microscope
rows: Single cell, moves with specialised structures
Spherical, comma, spiral or rod-shaped, hair-like projections

slides.title: What about viruses?
slides.body: **Viruses** are microscopic and **acellular** — they are not made of cells. A virus multiplies only after it **enters a living cell**, and it may infect plants, animals, or even bacterial cells and cause disease.

slides.title: How are we connected to microbes?
slides.intro: Have you seen a lemon, tomato, or orange rot after being left out? Powdery, cotton-like growth means microbes have moved in — and microbes are connected to us in many ways.

slides.title: Even your pickles tell a story
slides.body: Microorganisms are found everywhere — water, soil, air, and some food items — and show **great diversity** in shape, from spherical to rod-shaped to irregular. Some survive **extreme conditions** like hot springs and snow-cold zones. Many live inside us, especially the **bacteria in our gut** that help digestion. But why don't they spoil **pickles and murabbas**? Because the high concentration of **salt and sugar** acts as a preservative and stops them from growing.

slides.title: Key players in cleaning the environment
slides.intro: How does the diversity of microbes help clean the environment? Let us understand this by doing an activity.

slides.title: Turning kitchen peels into manure
slides.purpose: Where do fallen leaves and food peels disappear to? We bury fruit and vegetable peels in soil to watch **microbes recycle waste** into something useful.
steps: Fill — half-fill an empty container with garden soil
Add — put in fruit and vegetable peels, then cover with a layer of soil
Wait — leave it aside and, after 2–3 weeks, observe the change
slides.observe: The peels turn into a **dark-coloured material** called **manure**, rich in nutrients and able to increase the soil's fertility. Fungi and bacteria broke the plant waste into simpler, nutrient-rich substances — this is why gardeners pile dry leaves into pits.

slides.title: Decomposition keeps the world clean
slides.body: Microorganisms break down complex substances of fallen leaves and dead bodies into **simpler, nutrient-rich substances** — a process called **decomposition**. These nutrients go back to the soil and help plants grow better. So microbes not only help plants grow, they **clean our environment** by recycling waste — and manure forms best at the right temperature and moisture.

slides.translation: Ancient Indian texts, particularly the Vedas, refer to 'Krimi' — tiny entities both 'Drishya' (visible) and 'Adrishya' (invisible) — and mention their beneficial and harmful effects. The Atharvaveda also speaks of Krimi.

slides.title: From household waste to a pioneer of science
slides.leftBody: Many bacteria and fungi live in an **oxygen-free** environment and decompose plant, animal, and household waste. In doing so they release a gas mixture called **biogas**, rich in **methane** — used as fuel for cooking, heating, electricity, and even vehicles.
slides.rightBody: An Indian-born scientist who studied bacteria. In **1971** he developed a bacterium that could break down **oil spills**, and his discovery received a **patent in 1980**. His work showed how microorganisms could solve environmental problems like pollution.

slides.title: Microorganisms and food
slides.intro: How does the diversity of microbes help in our kitchen? Let us understand by performing activities in the kitchen.

slides.title: Why dough rises with yeast
slides.purpose: Why does dough become soft and fluffy? We set up a **fair test** — one bowl with yeast, one without — to see what the microbe actually does.
steps: Measure — take **200 g** of flour (atta or maida) in each of two bowls, A and B, with a pinch of sugar
Add yeast — mix a little **yeast** powder into bowl A only; leave bowl B plain for comparison
Knead — make soft dough in both with **warm water**, cover with a damp cloth, keep warm
Observe — check both bowls after 4–5 hours
slides.observe: Bowl A has **risen, become fluffy**, and smells different; bowl B has not. Yeast — a **fungus** — respires and breaks down the sugar, releasing **carbon dioxide** that makes bubbles, plus a little alcohol that gives the smell. This is how breads and cakes are made.

slides.title: Setting curd in warm and cold milk
slides.purpose: What conditions does milk need to become curd? We add curd to **warm** milk and **cold** milk to discover what the microbe needs.
steps: Set up — pour lukewarm milk in bowl A and cold milk in bowl B
Inoculate — add a small spoonful of **curd** to each bowl and mix well
Place — keep bowl A in a **warm** place and bowl B in a **cool** place (like a refrigerator)
Observe — after a few hours or overnight, compare the two and record predictions and observations
slides.observe: Milk in **bowl A turns into curd** and becomes a little sour; bowl B does not curdle. The curd carries **Lactobacillus** bacteria, which feed on the milk sugar (**lactose**), multiply, and produce **lactic acid** instead of alcohol — and they grow well only in **warm** conditions.

slides.title: Rhizobium fixes nitrogen for free
slides.body: Some bacteria, such as **Rhizobium**, live in swollen **root nodules** of legumes like beans, peas, and lentils. They **trap nitrogen from the air** and make it useful for the plant, so it grows well without chemical fertilisers. This is why farmers grow legumes **in rotation** — it naturally enriches the soil's nitrogen for the next crop.

slides.title: Amazing microalgae: tiny helpers in water
slides.intro: Microalgae are microscopic, plant-like organisms that make their own food using sunlight — and they do far more for us than their size suggests.

slides.title: Microalgae make more than half our oxygen
slides.body: **Microalgae** live in water, soil, air, and even on trees, making their own food from sunlight. While doing so they release **more than half of the Earth's oxygen** and are rich in nutrients, feeding many aquatic animals. Some — like **Spirulina**, **Chlorella**, and **Diatoms** — are used by humans as health supplements and medicines, help clean water, and make biofuel. But pollution and climate change threaten them, so conserving these tiny organisms protects Earth's oxygen balance.

slides.title: Spirulina, a superfood you can farm
slides.body: **Spirulina**, a microalga, is called a **superfood** — it is a good source of **vitamin B12** and is more than **60 per cent protein** by weight, with only a little fat and sugar. It can be farmed easily in a glass tank of pond water kept out of direct sunlight, becoming a real livelihood opportunity that supports food security.

slides.title: Why is cell considered to be a basic unit of life?
slides.intro: The body of every living organism is made of tiny building blocks called cells. Whether one cell or many, the cell is where life happens.

slides.title: Unicellular and multicellular life
slides.leftBody: Bacteria and protozoa carry out **every life process** in a **single cell**. Bacteria have no well-defined nucleus or nuclear membrane — only a region called a **nucleoid** — which sets them apart from yeast, protozoa, algae, fungi, plants, and animals.
slides.rightBody: Plants and animals are **many-celled**; their cells take on **specialised jobs** individually but also **cooperate** to improve the chance of survival. Yeast is a unicellular fungus, while mould is a multicellular fungus.

slides.title: There is far more inside a cell
slides.body: We have looked at only a few basic cell structures. A cell has many more components you will study in higher classes — and to see them we need stronger microscopes. An **electron microscope** magnifies a cell about **10,00,000 times**, revealing structures a light microscope can never show. The cell, in one form or many, truly is the **basic unit of life**.

slides.title: Words from this chapter
slides.body: The vocabulary of the invisible living world:

slides.title: The invisible world is everywhere
slides.subtitle: From cells in an onion peel to microbes that set your curd, raise your bread, feed plants, and clean the soil — tiny life keeps our world running. Ready to explore it yourself?
